title: OET Reading Practice Test 3
instructions: OET Reading has three parts. Part A: rapid reading across short healthcare texts. Part B: short workplace texts. Part C: two longer healthcare texts. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part A — Expeditious Reading
parts.description: Four short texts on a single healthcare topic; locate specific information quickly.

parts.title: Part B — Workplace Texts
parts.description: Short workplace documents (policies, manuals, guidelines, emails); identify the main point or purpose.

parts.title: Part C — Presentation Texts
parts.description: Two longer texts; detailed comprehension of opinion, attitude and meaning.

passages.title: Dehydration in Elderly Patients
passages.text: Dehydration is a common but often overlooked condition in older adults, contributing to confusion, falls, and hospital admissions. Elderly patients have reduced thirst sensation and may forget to drink, making them vulnerable to fluid loss. Common causes include diuretic medications, diarrhoea, vomiting, and reduced intake during acute illness. Signs of dehydration include dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor, decreased urine output, and elevated serum sodium levels. Confusion and delirium may be the only presenting symptom in frail elderly patients. Prevention through regular fluid intake, monitoring urine colour, and reducing diuretic use where possible is essential. Caregivers should offer fluids regularly with meals and snacks. Mild dehydration often responds to oral rehydration solutions, whilst moderate to severe cases require intravenous fluids and hospital monitoring.

passages.title: Infection Prevention in Aged Care Facilities
passages.text: Aged care facilities must implement strict infection control measures to protect vulnerable residents. All staff, residents, and visitors presenting with symptoms of infection should be screened and isolated if necessary. Outbreak protocols must be activated immediately if three or more residents develop symptoms within 72 hours. Cleaning staff must use appropriate disinfectants on all high-touch surfaces such as doorknobs, handrails, and bed rails daily. Residents should have access to hand sanitiser and be encouraged to perform hand hygiene. Annual influenza vaccinations are mandatory for all staff and recommended for all residents. Suspected outbreaks must be reported to the local health authority within 24 hours.

passages.title: Catheterisation Protocol
passages.text: Urinary catheterisation should only be performed when absolutely necessary due to risk of infection. Indications include acute urinary retention, monitoring of urine output in critically ill patients, and perioperative care. Before catheterisation, confirm there are no contraindications and obtain patient consent. Use aseptic technique throughout the procedure. The smallest appropriate catheter size should be selected, typically 12-14 French gauge for most adults. Document catheter size, type, insertion time, and urine characteristics. Catheters should be removed as soon as clinically appropriate, preferably within 48 hours. Daily catheter care includes perineal cleansing and inspection for signs of infection such as fever, dysuria, or turbid urine.

passages.title: Medication Adherence in Chronic Disease
passages.text: Poor medication adherence is a major contributor to treatment failure, hospital readmissions, and increased healthcare costs. Studies indicate that only 50% of patients take their medications as prescribed. Reasons for non-adherence are multifactorial and include side effects, cost, complexity of regimens, forgetfulness, and lack of understanding about the disease. Healthcare professionals must explore barriers during consultations rather than assuming non-compliance is deliberate. Simplifying regimens through combination therapies or once-daily formulations improves adherence. Providing written information, using pill organisers, and setting medication reminders through mobile phone applications have shown effectiveness. Regular follow-up appointments to monitor therapeutic response and adjust medications maintain engagement. Shared decision-making, where patients participate in treatment choices, significantly improves adherence rates. Healthcare systems that address cost barriers, such as subsidising essential medications, show better outcomes. The most effective approach combines patient education, simplified regimens, reminder systems, and ongoing support.

passages.title: Respiratory Hygiene and Cough Etiquette
passages.text: Respiratory infections spread primarily through droplets expelled when infected individuals cough or sneeze. Appropriate respiratory hygiene practices significantly reduce transmission of contagious diseases. Cough etiquette involves covering the mouth and nose with a tissue when coughing or sneezing, followed by immediate hand hygiene. If tissues are unavailable, coughing into the elbow is preferable to bare hands. Individuals with respiratory symptoms should maintain distance from others, ideally at least one metre. Healthcare workers and public health officials have a responsibility to model good hygiene practices and educate the community. Surgical masks reduce transmission when worn correctly by symptomatic individuals, blocking large respiratory droplets. N95 respirators provide better protection when worn by healthcare workers in close contact with confirmed or suspected cases. Masks are most effective as part of a comprehensive approach including isolation, ventilation improvements, and rapid diagnosis. During epidemic periods, mask use in public settings reduces disease transmission by up to 50%. Public health messaging should emphasise that respiratory hygiene protects vulnerable populations including infants, elderly, and immunocompromised individuals.
